utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, are you ready to continue your cross-examination or to resume your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom. I am afraid that for the first time in three years, I had forgotten to ask Madam Registrar to call the case, so would you please do so, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, Your Honours, this is IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Fortunately, no procedural step has been taken before calling the case so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I suppose if Your Honour had asked me if I was ready to continue and I gave a different answer, then I would upset Your Honour. The answer is yes I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, I'd like to remind you again, which may not come as a surprise, that you are still bound by the is solemn declaration that you have given at the beginning of your testimony, that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart. I had forgotten to remind you as well, but that whenever you are afraid that an answer could be -- could incriminate yourself, that you can address the Court and ask not to be obliged to answer that question. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, I wonder if you might be given, please, once again, a copy of your -- the transcript of the interview which you gave -- which was held in May of this year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May last year?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I do mean last year, of course. May this year would be difficult, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In the -- it's page 3 Your Honours, of that interview in the English version, and it's page 3, line 20, I think, in the B/C/S version. And Mr. Margetts raises with you there a question about the first and second laws of government. Just to refresh the first matter is Mr. Margetts, "The first matter I'd like to discuss with you is the organisation of the government in Republika Srpska in 1992 and the" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you please slow down while reading, Mr. Stewart. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- "and the relationship" I'm asked to slow down. "... and the relationship between the government and the other republic organs in Republika Srpska. I am handing to Mr. Trbojevic the first law on the government and then the second law on the government." Then at page 4 in the middle of page 4 of the English, and then page 4, line 21 of the B/C/S, you -- well, in fact, just a few lines before that, you're asked by Mr. Margetts, "Did the government function in accordance with those laws?" And then you said, "From the moment when I entered, and they were trying their best to keep hold of it." "What do you mean by that?" You said, "I don't have any concrete opinion. Ministries are listed, and their area of work, and acts that the government was bringing and the fashion in which each ministry in their own area work and government as a whole, it was in some way based on these decision, these laws." Mr. Trbojevic, first of all, when you say it was in some way based on these laws, do you mean that there was a worse situation than the -- perhaps the usual imperfect way of operation of any institution or any government or other large organs?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant the following: In the month of May when I arrived in Pale, the government, first of all, did not have premises of its own. I don't know whether all the members were already there at the time, but the basic preconditions are placed to sit in, to have a person type up the materials, print them out, all these preconditions were practically non-existent. The government didn't have a single typewriter at the time when I showed up there in May, 1992, not to speak of computers or any other technology. That is why I wanted to say that we are doing our best to do our jobs in a way that would be germane to normal functioning and organisation of work of such a body.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You write forward quite a long way in this -- the same transcript of this interview, and this is at page 38 of the English, and it's at -- is in the middle of page 38 of the English, and is at page 32, line 46 to 50. There is a -- Mr. Margetts asks a question, "Were you operating in 1992 as if only an imminent threat of war had been declared or were you operating as if a state of war had been declared?" Are you able to pick up that question of Mr. Margetts from the text that you have in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't found it yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, it should be somewhere between page 32, line 46 and page 33, line 7, if that helps you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You've got it. And then your answer begins, "We were working in state" - it must be "a state" - "We were working in a state of anarchy unfortunately." You see that answer, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The English word that is coming back to you in your own language is anarchy, are you talking about something different from the state of practical disorganisation, typewriters and so on that you were referring to a moment ago or are you embracing the whole situation in that word?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were discussing the way the government operated and I explained here that the regulations that we had were applicable for peacetime. The conditions of work for the government were practically unbearable. I explained that a lot of pressure had been coming from the military to declare a state of war, and in our opinion conditions were not in place for such a declaration to take place because first of all, we thought that an actual war was never going to break out. Secondly, if one declares a state of war, then one has to go over to a completely different system of organising work and life and I believe, at the time, we were -- we did not have the ability to carry it through so that on the one hand, the government did not have conditions in place to allow it to operate. On the other hand, there were events that were passing us by. And on the third side, there were these requests that -- for the declaration of a state of war and that is why I called the entire situation an anarchical one because it was a situation where things were not sorted out and where problems were difficult to solve.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So are you -- are they linked together in this way, Mr. Trbojevic, then, that there was anarchy in the way that you have just described it, and really as part of that overall situation, there was these sort of practical logistical disorganisation and shortage of resources that you described in relation to the conduct of government, no typewriters, that sort of thing. Is that -- is that a fair summary of your position?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is definitely one of its aspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And not dealing with specific typewriters, Mr. Trbojevic, but that situation of lack of practical resources, equipment, basic organisational facilities, when you arrived in Pale in May 1992, did that apply generally to the different organs and different branches of the running of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the general framework. We were all experiencing the same conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So all in that context, whether it was you or whether it was Mr. Djeric or whether it was Mr. Stanisic, in his ministry, Mr. Subotic in his ministry, Mr. Krajisnik at the Assembly, or Mr. Karadzic in his work, everybody was experiencing some such fairly difficult, in fact, very difficult problem of resources, equipment, organisation. Is that -- is that a fair summary?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: At page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you moving to a new subject, Mr. Stewart. I've just got a -- you started with page 3. Mr. Tieger, it's not without concern that I have to establish that page 3, line 20, as indicated by Mr. Stewart at least is in the English version partly unintelligible, whereas a lot of information seems to appear in the B/C/S version but not translated. If you compare that and I compare that with both versions, but it's worrying that the English version is -- seems not to be -- is not a translation of the B/C/S version so we are working with, I take it, one version which has been taken from the B/C/S recording where sometimes matters were better understood and the other one is from an English recording not being -- not corresponding completely. That's -- I wonder what to do with it. You understand what I mean? If you compare this first part Mr. Stewart has drawn our attention to, that you see that at least two lines with all kind of references are missing in the English. I'll give you the time, perhaps you think it over, and Mr. Stewart, perhaps could proceed meanwhile.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I should say, Your Honour does certainly put your finger on a real practical issue here in the text so we have been a bit troubled by this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But let's await some response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What the Prosecution says.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, at page 5, it is of the English version, and it's also page 5 of the B/C/S at lines 10 to 11, you were asked about your own contribution to the debate in the 20th Assembly, 20th Republika Srpska Assembly. Do you see that passage, Mr. Trbojevic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean the one starting on page 4 at line 46 and then going over to page 5, if that's the bit, then I'm with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, well that's -- you're trying to help me, Mr. Trbojevic. Problem I have with that is that the page and line references don't help me because I don't have the B/C/S to look at and can't read B/C/S. But does it refer to your being handed minutes of - by Mr. Margetts - minutes of the 20th session of the Assembly of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't say so. Yes, yes. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you recall, you -- it was suggested that a change should be proposed to the law so that the government would implement rather than conduct policy. This was in September 1992. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was it because -- well, up to then, if that change came in 1992, that would imply that the government had previously, under the law, had the responsibility for conducting policy; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the other way around. The situation was the opposite. We were discussing amendments to the law and it was envisaged that a provision would be put in place to the effect that the government was implementing the policy just as the case had been before. My suggestion was that the government ought to conduct, pursue the policy for the duration of its term of office. This, of course, meant that the political frame works would be determined by the Assembly but that then the government would have both the responsibility and the possibility to run the policy. However, this was not met with support and the government's status of implementing the policies given to it prevailed. And this was what the practice had been before. In essence, this was more of a theoretical discussion than a practical one because this matter had never even been raised as a controversial one but since the discussion talked -- was about the amendments to the bill, I decided to raise this issue and to provoke discussion on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So the position was you were -- well, you were clearly in a minority on this particular issue; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite right. I was in a minority, entirely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you see your position as intending to bring about a change?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So your position is that the government was not in any sense conducting policy before this debate occurred in the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is explained in this interview of mine further on where I stated that the government was virtually a service, the task of which was to implement whatever had been put to it as its task without having the possibility to decide upon matters -- to decide upon policies, that is. My proposal as you see it here was more of a protest, really, against the then current state of affairs because I did not really think that it was going to be endorsed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You're referring, are you, Mr. Trbojevic, when you talk about your interview, to the passage which is found on page 5 of the English, the middle of the first long paragraph, and in the B/C/S at page 5, very top, lines 2 to 4, I think it should be, where you say, "The government was treated as the most banal executor of the political attitudes." Do you see that phrase?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. And further on to line 10 and 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Let's just go up a couple of lines to get the context of the -- I'll go to the middle of this answer, but you say, "That was my personal opinion because I was partly provoked by the problems of the government. Because government was treated as the most banal executor of the political attitudes ..." And I'll just pause there for a moment. So that's your protest, as you described it. You were provoked by the situation and you felt you wanted to assert this view.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And publicly assert it, of course, in the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, that was the most appropriate place for doing so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then you go on to say here, "Because" -- that passage then about the government being the most banal executor of the political attitudes continues, "The political attitudes which either like would SDS have or the Assembly had, or the Presidency. So, in that way, the government was supposed to be some practical service and like, the government was just supposed to conduct some tasks that were given to it." So the English version is not entirely a happy passage in English but there are three elements, if you like, political attitudes of the SDS, or the Assembly, or the Presidency. And can you confirm that the B/C/S version of what you said does reflect those three possibilities being contained in that proposition?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So what you're saying in a nutshell is that somebody other than the government was setting policy; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And it was the SDS or the Assembly or the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was practically one and the same thing. The Assembly was almost 100 per cent composed of the deputies of the SDS. The Presidency was -- comprised the highest, the most senior officials of Republika Srpska so that the -- whatever policies were set, they were set by the same authors.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So you're describing a situation in which the Assembly, as we know the Assembly, had overwhelming majority, really, overwhelming majority of SDS deputies, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The Presidency consisted of SDS members?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The Assembly was, as in many parliamentary democracies, the Assembly was unlikely not to reflect pretty loyally and consistently SDS party attitudes, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Would there be any reason to suppose at that time that the government as constituted would not also reflect SDS party attitudes because of the composition of the government?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government was set up at the time when one did not really pay that much attention to the fact whether government members were also members of the SDS. I cannot tell you now how many government members were actually SDS members and how many weren't. Following these discussions of outside, although they did not really amount to any hostile confrontations, the SDS probably concluded that the government should, in the future, comprise only SDS cadre and that those who were not SDS members would not be able to become government members, Mr. Velibor Ostojic informed us thereof and he practically threatened to the effect that those who were not SDS members and were not the party faithful would not be in the government. I have to tell you the following: This did not amount to any fundamental disagreement in such a situation where nothing was in order. The government did not wish to be marginalised in the face of some decisions being taken as to what the policies and the goals of the activities are and this specific discussion was, to put it mildly, just an attempt to try and draw their attention to this very fact, that it wasn't expedient for the government to be a third-rate executioner of some insignificant tasks but that it should rather be enabled to have a more active and serious role, if any serious results were to be expected from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Trbojevic, for all its no doubt imperfections and for all the difficulties of the anarchic situation, as you've described it, Republika Srpska was, in essence, constitutionally, it was a parliamentary democracy, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you wouldn't suggest that there was anything sinister nor indeed politically unusual about a government being constituted in such a way that it would very largely reflect the political attitudes of the party which overwhelmingly controlled the parliament?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, you've got a -- we're agreed you've got a parliament in this or an assembly in this parliamentary democracy, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And that parliament, I'll call it, is overwhelmingly controlled as a matter of voting by one particular party, the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And in fact, constitutionally, when it -- if it came to the crunch, members of the government might be appointed or removed individually by the Prime Minister but the whole government was subject, ultimately, to the Assembly which could remove the government; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So in those circumstances, a government which closely reflected in political attitudes the political attitudes of the Assembly and therefore the political attitudes of the party that controlled the Assembly would be the normal, natural political expectation, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government did not strictly reflect party affiliation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, let me stop you there, please, Mr. Trbojevic, and I'm not stopping you from answering my question, the exact opposite, I wish you to answer my question. My question referred to a government which not strictly but closely reflected in political attitudes the attitudes of the Assembly and the controlling party. That would be a natural political result in the circumstances, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And I think you indicated, but please tell the Trial Chamber if this is wrong, I think you indicated, Mr. Trbojevic, that in fact there weren't any significant policy differences or differences of political attitude between the government and the Assembly and the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there weren't any significant differences except for the fact that the government was the most poorly informed segment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Who was the -- you've referred to "segments," so the segments you're talking about, if we list them, do you mean the Assembly, the Presidency, those are two of the segments or different organs, are they, that you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we understand one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So the Assembly, the Presidency, the government, do you count the SDS as a party, as a separate segment or is it covered by those three?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a matter of assessment depending on how one likes to express oneself. What was defined in the Assembly and the Presidency was also defined in the party and most probably vice versa.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We'll probably get into some arid theoretical discussion if we pursue that point further, Mr. Trbojevic, but you've referred to the government as being "the most poorly informed of those segments," that's a convenient word you use. Which of those segments was the best informed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the Presidency was the best informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And on what facts do you base that assessment?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the fact that the members of the Presidency had contacts with international representatives. They participated in talks with international representatives. They went to Belgrade and it was always they who informed everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So there, you are talking about information, and you're saying they have -- the Presidency has better information coming from international representatives, and then you say Belgrade, they went to Belgrade. So you're using Belgrade, are you, as a shorthand for what or whom?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know there were contacts with President Milosevic. Yesterday, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. we saw a document showing that the Minister of the Police was in Belgrade attending a meeting. I know that there were contacts in the -- along the military line, and that would be it, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you talk about contacts along the military line, contacts between whom and whom?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday, I was describing the situation when materials were being prepared for the passing of a law on the army, how the members of the General Staff, how they had their contacts and what contacts they had, I don't know, but I assume that the Minister of Defence had to be kept abreast of all that, and through him, the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So first of all you assume that the Minister of Defence had to be kept abreast. Kept abreast by the General Staff or by whom?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's something that I'm not assuming; I know, to a large extent. I know that he maintained contacts with the members of the general staff, that they came to see him, that they also came to the Presidency, both General Mladic and General Tolimir, and General Gvero as well. I know that Colonel Subotic went to see General Mladic in Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So your complaint, as it seems to be a complaint, Mr. Trbojevic, your complaint is not that -- not that Mr. Subotic kept himself and was kept abreast of such matters, that's -- you -- that's what you would have expected and supported, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't bothered by that. I didn't see that it was a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it was not normal for the government not to know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, I'm taking this in stages, Mr. Trbojevic, so that you can clearly explain to us your position. You not only couldn't have any complaint about Mr. Subotic keeping himself abreast and being kept abreast of such matters, but he was the Minister of Defence. As the Deputy Prime Minister, you would have been entitled to complain if he hadn't kept himself abreast, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, both the Prime Minister and the Deputy Prime Minister had no competencies in the area of national defence; however, it -- there was a state of war. Everything was on fire, so to say, all around us, and we didn't know which of the ministers was working on which side. Simply it seemed essential that if we were going to set up a government, we had to know how people ticked and what they were going to do. I allow that there were certain topics which were not such that they should have been broadcast to everyone but we felt that this was a problem. It's a fact that Branko Djeric, the Prime Minister, did not go to Belgrade, either did the president of Serbia or the president of Yugoslavia and did not attend a single meeting with either of them or have any kind of talks with them or cooperate where them in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So your concern or complaint was this, was it, that having been kept abreast and keeping himself informed as Minister of Defence, Mr. Subotic then conveyed disproportionate amount of information to Dr. Karadzic as opposed to you and his government colleagues?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I have said that more than once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the witness has, I think, said this some four or five times, including yesterday, Mr. Stewart. I'd like to -- because on the basis of his testimony of yesterday and -- Mr. Stewart asked you and you correctly answered, you had said already a couple of times that your problem was that the information was not shared with you as cabinet ministers and then Mr. Stewart said that you -- that your complaint was that Mr. Subotic then conveyed disproportionate amount of information to Dr. Karadzic as opposed to you and his government colleagues. Was it about Mr. Karadzic or was it that Mr. Subotic shared this information with others than Karadzic as well? Was it exclusively Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From conversations with Colonel Subotic, I know this. Mostly, he went to see the chief, that was the expression he used, to refer to Dr. Karadzic. Most often, what he would say in such situations was that he had reported to the chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your earlier testimony today was, and I'm reading it, "I know that he maintained contacts with the members of the General Staff, that he came to see him, that they also came to the Presidency, both General Mladic and General Tolimir, and General Gvero as well. I know that Colonel Subotic went to see General Mladic in Han Pijesak." He said he went to the chief. In earlier parts of your testimony, you have talked about sharing information with the Presidency, with others as well. Was it -- did you gain the impression from what he said that he was exclusively sharing the information from Mr. Karadzic or was it a wider circle or were there more persons he would share it with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to what he said, he often said, not every time, but very often, he said he had briefed the chief or the boss, meaning Karadzic. To what extent the other members of the Presidency were informed, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In your earlier answers, you refer to the Presidency in this respect as well. Were those answers not correct or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, in everyday speech, when someone said, "I'm going to the Presidency," this implied the four of them. Djeric was in another building and it was Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, Mrs. Plavsic, and Mr. Koljevic who were together in that building. So when somebody said, "I've been to the Presidency, I've conveyed a message," or whatever, this meant the Presidency. Whether it was a meeting held at the Presidency or whether it took some other form, no one ever had reason to ask as distinct from some cases when Subotic would say, "I've given this to the chief or the boss," whenever he said that, we knew he was referring to Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart. I see Judge Hanoteau ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Earlier on, Mr. Stewart talked about the way the Assembly worked. If I understand what you said correctly, not all members of the Assembly were also members of the SDS; is that right? They were not all members of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to the democratic operation of the Assembly, I have a question. I'd like to know whether anyone was able to take the floor, give his or her opinion, or make suggestions. Was that possible? Was it possible for anyone to share -- to present a view that was not in line with the view of the majority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, they could do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your first statement, you said, and maybe you could look at this statement, page 21, do you have the text in front of you, the statement from March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's 583A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 21, do you have the page in front of you, page 21 in English. And you stated, talking about 1992, [In English] "Yes. I must tell you that this disagreements or disputes that started to be noticed at the time led to reaction of SDS. SDS asked that the Main Board, the SDS Main Board was also present at the Assembly sessions, which meant, to a certain number of delegates a sort of pressure."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't found it yet but I do remember that I said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This seems to imply -- well, I don't know, what is your interpretation because maybe I misunderstood that passage? But the impression I got was that you meant that freedom of speech was not maybe as -- what it should have been.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, it was certainly a form of pressure. I can't say it was something very real, but when you have 70 SDS deputies and as many members of the main SDS board and then two or three people get up and say they don't share their opinion, and everybody starts yelling at them, provoking them, and so on and so forth, even threatening them, although none of this was very realistic, but it was certainly not a very pleasant experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you maintain that it was possible for anyone to speak freely? Because that's what was your first answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We did speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At page 21, you stated the following when you talked about an event I'm not going to recall in detail, page 22, you state, that during meetings of the SDS main board, [In English] So there was no chance to even start a discussion in the Assembly in the Assembly about other proposals that what Karadzic and Krajisnik were persistent in pursuing. [Interpretation] Forgive me because I might have misinterpreted what you said but the impression I got was that when it was not at the Assembly, you were discouraged to bring up at the Assembly subjects of discussions that were different from what had been decided at the beginning and that it went very far because if you did that, then you were treated as traitors to the party or to the ideology. What did you really mean here when you said that, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is something I talked about a moment ago. There were cases where you would be publicly called a traitor, a person who cannot -- no longer be trusted and this dissuaded the people from joining the discussion if they were opposed to the mainstream issue. I saw Toholj's name here. Toholj picked out me and several colleagues of us and called us traitors, Mr. Krajisnik, who was the chairman, spoke against such qualifications; however, we felt uncomfortable all the same because it's not really pleasant for someone to be called a traitor, a person who cannot be trusted by a multitude of people in a room and especially during a state of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said -- you then say the following: [In English] "Krajisnik who was presiding the meeting takes me personally under his protection as a person who was good, valuable, important, without any personal interests in this business, but very soon, it turned out that I was expelled from the Assembly." [Interpretation] Could you please explain to me what all this means? What did you mean by "expelled from the Assembly"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember saying or seeing this bit here, that Krajisnik took me under his protection. One of the organs of the SDS, whether the Executive Board or some other party body passed a conclusion whereby I, as a deputy, was to be given a vote of censure and deprived of my term of office. I showed up at one of the sessions where Velibor Ostojic read this conclusion out and, of course, I stood up and left. The underlying explanation was that my speeches, my remarks were disrupting the operation of the Assembly or something along that line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Following to what you've just said in answer to my questions, can you tell me if you believe that the Assembly was working democratically, according to democratic principles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Within the framework of the Serbian Democratic Party, or rather as far as the party allowed it to be democratic, it was democratic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one additional question in relation to this. Was there any legal basis for expelling you from the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am deeply convinced that there was none. This subject matter was regulated by law but due to the state of war and these circumstances, the practice went beyond the provisions of the law when it came to the extension of the term of office, and a new piece of legislation at the time had not yet been adopted so that under these circumstances, this was a fully unlawful decision. However, one was unable to challenge it at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did anyone oppose your expulsion from the Assembly? Was there any Assembly member or any government member or any Presidency member, was there any political authority or -- that opposed against your expulsion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were four of us who were expelled on that occasion in the same way and nobody opposed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were all of you non-SDS members, all of the four, I meant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not, but I cannot be certain about the others. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, could you please make it specifically clear to the Trial Chamber when it was that you were expelled from the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Much later, not in 1992. It happened, if I'm not mistaken, in the summer of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what -- without encouraging you to go into enormous length, Mr. Trbojevic, if you were tempted, what, in summary, was the issue which led to your expulsion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision on the expulsion or rather on the withdrawal of my term of office did not contain any specific reasons. I also must add that I never received -- I never saw a decision -- the decision in writing, but I saw one of the decisions relating to another colleague of mine. There was nothing specific, merely that with our remarks, we disrupted the unity of the Assembly, or something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Trbojevic, I'm going to have to press you a little. Four members of an Assembly of parliament are expelled by their colleagues, and you were one of them. I must, please, urge you to tell the Trial Chamber something of what you must know as to the reasons for the four of you being expelled.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you because they were not put on paper. I was unable to read them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any reason which you had in mind which might not have been put on paper? Did anyone ever tell you or did you have any suspicion of what was the issue that may finally have led to your expulsion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot tell you this, really. At this 22nd session, we, meaning the government, were dissolved because it was maintained that the government had to have strictly party people. Later on, there were discussions at the Assembly sessions where I put forth some positions that were not generally accepted by the Assembly. Now, the drop which might have spilled over the cup of patience of the SDS, I cannot tell you which one it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you have two or three drops in mind, just briefly mention them so that we could -- it might help Mr. Stewart to find the proper answer. Mr. Stewart just wants to know whether you have any idea what was the disagreement, what was the incident, what was the issue on which certain people thought that it would be better to expel you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was several such situations, one of them was when a number of laws were being drafted covering significant walks of life in -- especially where they wanted to put forth the same provisions that would apply both to the imminent threat of war and the state of war. I disagreed with such a decision and I expressed by disagreement and was then asked to leave the session. In my opinion, to allow different organs of the state to function in a state which was not declared as a state of war, to function as if they were in a state of war, I thought that this was not going to lead to a very good organisation of life in the society and this was a thorn in the side of the SDS. There were debates surrounding the adoption of the Vance-Owen Plan. I believe I was the only deputy to express the view that if the condition was that the International Community was not going to put in place any sanctions against us and if the condition was that Serbia did not have to apply sanctions against us if the peace agreement was signed, then in that case, one did not have to have any second thoughts about it. The agreement had to be signed and then the negotiations were to be pursued in order to settle as many issues. The last drop might have been, if I remember well, at one Assembly session that was held at the time more or less when I was expelled. Mr. Karadzic was reporting on the state of affairs with regard to the negotiations. He used, among others, the following formulation: "We have been receiving signals from around the world that we should try and endure for some time still and we will achieve our goals." In reaction to this, I took the floor and said the following: "Radovan, we cannot give support unless we have something that is more substantial. You have to tell us what sort of signals you're receiving and by whom. We cannot give support or endorse something or somebody if we don't know what or who that is." I could tell by the expression on his face that he was bothered by this remark of mine. It perhaps wasn't very diplomatic and this might have been the last drop, although, I repeat, it might have been. Nobody said anything specific to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, we heard some potential drops. I do not know whether you are going to inquire into another one, but please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's most helpful, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, all these drops that accumulated in the bucket and spilled over, we're talking about 1994 in relation to all this particular dispute, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. The events I was relaying date back to both 1993 and 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you were -- two things happened, did they, you, with other members of the government, were removed from your government positions; that happened, did it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Branko Djeric resigned at the Assembly session in -- held in November. As a result, the entire government was removed. This was in November 1992. Of the deputies who were excluded from the Assembly in 1994, I believe it was 1994, sometime in the summer, one member of the SDS was also expelled, that was Radovan Brdjanin. Several months later, it was the turn of the four of us. At that time, none of us were government members anymore, we were deputies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: This is what I'm just trying to get clear, please, Mr. Trbojevic. You left the government of Mr. Djeric, of course, in November 1992; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In January of 1993, because the government had to go on operating until the election of a new one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You then remained as a deputy until your expulsion in 1994; that's clear, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And your answer, when His Honour asked you about the legality of your expulsion as a deputy, was that your view was that there wasn't a, I think, legal basis was His Honour or very close to what His Honour asked you, that there wasn't a legal basis. You are a lawyer, of course, Mr. Trbojevic. Are you -- let's distinguish two things, please: Are you saying that there was not a legal machinery for a deputy to be expelled or that, in your view, that machinery was abused in your case because there wasn't a proper reason for expelling you. Which of the two? You understand the distinction, first, do you, Mr. Trbojevic? I'm sorry, I don't wish to be patronising, just to be clear. You understand the distinction I'm making, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see what that has got to do with this case. But anyway, we were nominated and elected. May I answer the question, Your Honour? We were nominated and elected in accordance with the electoral law that was in force in 1990, I believe. It was pursuant to this law that the national Assembly was elected. Under this law, there was a procedure providing for the revocation of the elected deputies. This was a rather unpractical procedure which meant that the deputy could be revoked the same way he had been elected, by the direct vote of the electorate which was almost impossible in organisational terms. Meanwhile, as I've stated, the term of office of the entire Assembly of all the deputies was extended because the state of affairs at the time made it impossible to hold free elections. The National Assembly passed a new law on elections where the issue of party representatives was regulated differently. The candidates were no longer placed on lists individually with their names, nor were they actually elected individually; rather, the vote was cast in relation to the entire list. It was therefore provided that in proportion to the number of the candidates, the number of the votes that a list got in the election that some of the -- a certain number of the candidates, as they were put on the list, would be given seats in the Assembly, whereas a different number of seats could be elected or rather selected by the party itself. It had the discretionary power to do so depending on the persons who were on the list and depending on the functions that they would eventually be assigned. This law, therefore, also provided for the possibility that the party might exchange some of the deputies that had been given a seat by that party. Now, at that point when a decision was taken to take our terms of office away, a certain body of the party met which did not have any competencies under the party statute. There was no procedure that was carried out, no decision was taken, no criteria were taken into consideration by this body. Like for instance the criterion as to whether I had been chosen from the list, from the top part of the list or the lower part of the list because you were to be given a seat in the Assembly depending on the rank that you -- on how high you were ranked on the list. One could not tamper with that. So a letter was sent to the Assembly informing it that this body had decided to withdraw the mandate, the term of office of the following persons and there our names were mentioned. I don't think I could have been more brief in explaining this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic has taken us through to the break now, perhaps. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I have one small question just in verification, to understand. In the system, a system which you described as a democratic system, it was finally the party that could replace Assembly members by others.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, perhaps -- do you consider that a democratic system where finally the party could do so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It entirely depends on the concept. There's no reason for it not to be democratic because the party got the votes and it has the freedom to dispose of them. Because under the law, one -- a certain percentage of those contained on the list would get the seats automatically, whereas the other percentage was left to the discretionary power of the party. Since I was rated fifth out of, I believe 140, there was no way that my name could have been manipulated. I was fifth, sixth, or seventh; I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You claimed that your place on the list entitled you to a -- well, let's say, non-replaceable seat in the Assembly; is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. Besides, this law could not have been applied at all to an Assembly that had been constituted under the old law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that you consider that there was a problem in transition of the laws in terms of time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will adjourn until a quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, shortly before the break or a little while before the break, anyway, you were being asked or it was being summarised for you a passage in your earlier interview, the March 2004 interview, at page 21 of the English, I don't have the reference to this, but it's a very short passage to remind you of. You said that "the SDS" -- I must tell you, I think His Honour Judge Hanoteau read this passage to you: "I must tell you that disagreements or disputes that started to be noticed at that time led to reaction of SDS. SDS asked that the Main Board -- the SDS Main Board was also present at the Assembly sessions which meant to a certain number of delegates a sort of pressure." That you described as being in 1992. Could you be as specific as you can about when in 1992 you say that took place?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't be more specific. It can probably be seen in the minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- was the position this: That you said there were about 70 SDS delegates in the Assembly, a number of those, of course, Mr. Trbojevic, would have been members of the Main Board anyway, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think the deputies were members of the Main Board; maybe a few of them were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You'd agree -- I'm not concerned about precise numbers here, Mr. Trbojevic. Some of them were members of the Main Board, there was an overlap, wasn't there? Or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that's the case, but it's a fact that when the Main Board of the party attended a session, there were people sitting in the hall, there were twice as many of them, that is, than when only deputies were attending a session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And are you suggesting, Mr. Trbojevic, that -- that this was intended, that the invitation or the instruction, whatever it was, to SDS Main Board members to be present at the Assembly session, that this was intended in some way to put pressure on delegates?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the explanation that was given was so that both the deputies and the Main Board of the party would be better informed and that there could be a discussion among all of us which would make it easier to arrive at a unified standpoint. But as I explained, it did have the character of pressure, pressure was exerted on the deputies in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: On SDS deputies or non-SDS deputies or both?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think both.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So far as the non-SDS deputies are concerned, there was a clear political pressure anyway, wasn't there, in the form of the overwhelming parliamentary majority of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You said in your interview, and it would be in the second interview, page 7 in the English, I can't give a precise reference here, but it would be page 7 of the English and it would be page 6 of the -- I think you've got the second interview, haven't you, Mr. Trbojevic; it would be page 6 of that one. You said that the Main Board of that party, and the SDS is the one you were talking about, "... was like practically council of the Assembly." I'll try and get that passage for you. Do you see a question by Mr. Margetts that refers to the figure 90 per cent? It's got 90 per cent in the middle of a four-line question; do you see that? It will be on page 6 or 7, I think, that you're looking at. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, perhaps on page 7, approximately the seventh or the eighth line.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You found it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have found it. What was your question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's my reference point, Mr. Trbojevic. If you then go up ten lines up from that in the longer answer that you've just given before that question, there's a sentence referring to the Main Board, the English is, "But that was absolutely not true because the Main Board of that party was like practically Council of the Assembly." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could you explain what you meant there by saying it was "like practically Council of the Assembly."

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the way we broached this stop I can was by saying that political parties were supposed to cease their activities until the war ended and Karadzic often said that he had made a mistake in putting the activities of the SDS on hold while the activities were going on in the war theatre, and that the party was less active and did not operate. What I'm saying here is that this was not true because the party activities were not put on hold. Nobody insisting on the party ceasing its activities; on the contrary, I said that they were practically a Council of the Assembly. What I was trying to say was that the members of the board attended meetings of the deputies and participated on an equal footing in all the debates, and the tendency was for the Main Board of the party to tell the deputies what they should be doing and that the deputies themselves were not expected to say much about this. That's what I was trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, I -- just, with respect, I feel, perhaps, that you're not entirely focussing on the questions I'm putting sometimes so maybe I could invite you to listen very specifically to what I'm saying and answer the question as put. The -- I was asking you to explain what you meant by saying that "the Main Board was practically the Council of the Assembly." You've given some interesting, if you like, background and perhaps context but specifically on that point, what Council of the Assembly, what -- if it was like the Council of the Assembly, what do you mean by Council of the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I will read part of the answer. After some introduction, he said, "I said that they were practically Council of the Assembly. What I was trying to say was that the members of the board attended meetings of the deputies and participated on an equal footing in all the debates and the tendency was for the Main Board of the party to tell the deputies what they should be doing and that the deputies, themselves, were not expected to say much about this." I consider it not entirely fair to the witness to say that he did not listen to your question and he did not respond to your question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I think perhaps, Your Honour, with respect, Your Honour is right about that. So I was conversely wrong about that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you want to put another question to the witness, no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think that's entirely fair, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So you're not talking about any formal or even semi-formal organ here, it's just the description you've given of -- of how this involvement of Main Board worked.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was speaking of the de facto situation. I use this expression as a metaphor, as an illustration. I did not intend to refer to any formal body.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm going to, Mr. Trbojevic, I'm not able, but I don't think it's necessary to put this particular document in front of you, I'm going to read you a description of the Main Board's position and functions which comes from, and I in fairness should tell you where it comes from, it comes from an expert report produced by and for the Prosecution by a Mr. Patrick Treanor and just see how far you can agree with what Mr. Treanor said in his report. And the first one is about eight lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was in paragraph 31 for the reference of Mr. Treanor's report. What he said was this or what he wrote, "Indeed, the Main Board's activities are not very well-documented and as suggested by the lack of documentation, its meetings may not have been particularly frequent or regular. Despite the importance assigned to the Main Board by the party's Statutes, therefore, the central party body was overshadowed in the first year of the SDS's existence on the one hand, by the ad hoc decision-making procedures adopted by the party leadership in practice and on the other, by its much smaller executive body."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now that's the end of the passage. I should, in fairness to you, Mr. Trbojevic, remind you that talking about the first year of the SDS's existence of course we're not talking about 1992, we're talking about 1990 through to 1991. Do you, in fact, know anything about the Main Board and its activities during that first year of the SDS which puts you in a position to make any helpful comment at all on that passage from Mr. Treanor's report?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about the activities of the Main Board of the SDS from the time it was constituted up to the time they began to appear at sessions of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then another fairly short passage which is from paragraph 41 of Mr. Treanor's report, but not confined to that earlier period. He said, "Although the Main Board, of which Karadzic was it's ex officio chairman and Krajisnik was a particularly influential member was envisioned in the 1991 draft Statutes as the highest party body between sessions of the Assembly, the Executive Board continued to play a much more active role as a body. In practice though, neither of these formal party bodies regularly and consistently exercised control over the SDS structures." That's the end of the quote. Again, Mr. Trbojevic, do you have enough knowledge yourself to make a comment as to the accuracy or not of that passage?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I was not a member of the party and I don't have any knowledge about the cooperation, or lack of it, of the bodies within the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So when you referred in that answer that led to the brief exchange between His Honour Judge Orie and me, you said, "What I was trying to say was that the members of the board," that's the Main Board, "attended meetings of the deputies and participated on an equal footing in all debates. And the tendency was for the Main Board of the party to tell the deputies what they should be doing." The first question arising out of that, Mr. Trbojevic, is when you say, "... the members of the Main Board participated on an equal footing in all debates," you're saying that's strictly accurate that once non-deputy members of the Main Board were there at the Assembly, they, in practice, were every bit as free and in practice used that freedom every bit as much as deputies to speak in the Assembly, are you? Or don't you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for my clarification, Mr. Stewart. May I just ask you the following. When Mr. Stewart read to you," ... attended meetings of the deputies," that's what he read to you and then in his question he said, "... non-deputy members of the Main Board were there at the Assembly. They, in practice, were every bit as free." By "meeting of the deputies," did you mean to refer to formal Assembly meetings or would meeting of deputies be a wider concept, that means meeting of deputies out, apart from any formal Assembly meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a rule -- when I first mentioned this, I said that the member of the party Main Board attended members of the deputies' club which preceded the Assembly session. At the meeting of the deputies' club, they had a preliminary debate about what would be put on the agenda and what each item of the agenda would contain. It was the members of the Main Board who were not deputies as well as those deputies who belonged to the deputies' club who participated in the debate on an equal footing. I think that as for the formal official sessions of the Assembly, the members of the Main Board attended those only once or twice. It was not the practice for them to sit with us at the session itself, at least not all the time. Perhaps they did occasionally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if they were present in Assembly meetings, would they there also participate in the debate on an equal footing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, their attitude was the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honour, for Mr. Trbojevic's benefit, yes, my question had been framed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If I reference specifically to debates because -- Mr. Trbojevic, it's quite plain, isn't it, the only debates at which you personally were present and could make any observation were the Assembly sessions, weren't they, as opposed to the other sort of meeting.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also attended meetings of the deputies' club as well as sessions of the Assembly when I was there. I didn't attend them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So this was SDS deputies' club to which you were invited; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And were the relatively small number, I think, but were the other non-SDS delegates in the Assembly also invited to SDS deputies' club meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for a time, yes, they were because while the term that was predominantly used was "Serb deputy," this was unofficial, but that was what they were labelled, afterwards, they asked to set up a separate club of independent deputies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, who asked to set up a separate club of independent deputies?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several deputies, as far as I can remember 7 of them, and these were -- I've forgotten the names of the parties. The Independent Social Democrats, I think was the name -- you can't help me here. I can't remember all the names but it was the former Communists and the social democrats. There were several of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, perhaps that's not so critically important, anyway. Thank you. It's -- when you -- I think you said they were asked to form a separate deputies' club or something like that, the -- it was that that small group itself took the initiative, was it, to form itself into a deputies' club of independent members?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, they did form their club in agreement with the president of the Assembly and the secretary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that there is some confusion, Mr. Trbojevic. Mr. Stewart tries to find out who took the initiative that the -- well, let's say the independent members, the non-SDS members would no longer participate in the meetings of the deputies' club, the Serb deputies' club but would form their own deputies' club. Who initiated this by requesting or by taking an initiative?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The initiative came from the independent deputies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you said -- yes. So when you said "They asked," is that they sought permission to create their own deputies' club?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And when His Honour put that phrase to you, with respect, I have no objection or problem with that, but when His Honour talked about permission, was the position this, that in the first place, nobody's permission was needed for a group of independent deputies to meet among themselves whenever they wanted. That's a starting point, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, there are rules of procedure in the Assembly. I can't ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, perhaps I could be allowed, if you have an opportunity, perhaps I could be allowed to perhaps try and steer this with a series of questions and see whether we get there. First of all, this group -- nobody could stop them from, for example, just meeting in one of their own houses or hiring a room and they could meet, couldn't they? Nobody could or would stop them from doing that, would they? That's got to be a yes or no, Mr. Trbojevic, I would respectfully suggest.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody would prevent them from doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If they wanted to call themselves the Deputies' Club of Independent Members, no one could or would stop them from doing that either; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've tried to explain to you that there is the Assembly's rules of procedures which says how many deputies there have to be in order to -- for a club to be set up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, if you would let the witness answer the question. So you said in the rules of procedure, it says how many deputies you would need to set up a club. Yes. Any further questions on this, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What I was coming to then was, having established those two simple facts, Mr. Trbojevic, but in order for that group to be recognised then by the Assembly and recognised in dealings with Mr. Krajisnik, for example, as president of the Assembly, then it did need, in some formal sense, to be a deputies' club within the Assembly. That's what you're saying, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I put first a question. Was the number required under the rules, was it there or was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't tell you now off the cuff what the number was, but the number was definitely provided for. At the beginning, there was the provision whereby all of us were to fall under one club as deputies of the Serbian people because it was under that heading, so to speak, that we had walked out of the Bosnian Assembly. Later on, this group that called itself independent deputies expressed its desire to set up its own club, to have its own materials, and to have its deputies' club president raising matters at the Assembly session, to have its own premises where the club would meet, and all of this was carried out without the opposition from the SDS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you said there were seven non-SDS members.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was this a sufficient number to set up your own deputies' club according to the rules?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't claim either way. I can't say this now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we do not know whether, under the rules, it was as a right that they could create their deputies' club or whether an exception to the rules should be made for that purpose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But in any case, whichever it was, it appears clear from what you're saying, Mr. Trbojevic, that there was no lack of cooperation from Mr. Krajisnik or anybody else for that matter in recognition of and dealings with that deputies' club.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Just turning back to the Main Board, you described the Main Board as giving instructions to the deputies; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that the Main Board issued instructions, I said that the Main Board members attended the parliamentary debate with the deputies, presented their views, and, in this way, influenced the positions to be later on discussed or adopted by the deputies at an Assembly session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But these SDS meetings, you -- you -- did you get yourself invited to SDS deputies' club meetings from immediately after you arrived in Pale in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And was there -- of course there was eventually your expulsion from parliament, but throughout 1992, were you invited to SDS deputies' club meetings? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You see your answer, I was just looking for it a moment ago, your answer given, and it's at page 34 on everybody's screen at line 10, 16:27:01, the time, you said, "The tendency was for the Main Board of the party to tell the deputies what they should be doing and that the deputies themselves were not expected to say much about this." So it was clear you were saying there, it wasn't the Main Board. A moment ago, you seemed to be saying something slightly different. Perhaps we can make it clear. Are you saying from your own observation that the Main Board of the SDS as an organ had the tendency to tell the deputies what they should be doing?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know whether the Main Board, as a body, had earlier on adopted some conclusions that were to be later on through parliamentary debates imposed upon the deputies. I don't know of any such case. I don't think there was ever a situation where a person would stand up and say the Main Board has decided and then read out something along the lines of an order. I don't think there was ever such a case. But that a group of people, some 50, 60 people would enter the conference room and advocate certain views, well, I, myself, perceived that as pressure because, if there's a large number of people confronting me, then that leads me to that feeling that I have already talked about here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Help me be clear, Mr. Trbojevic, then, throughout the second half of May 1992, June, July, August, September 1992, were you and the other independent delegates all invited to meetings of the SDS deputies' club?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of us were invited.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there any point at which only one or some of you came to be invited?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of any such situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there any point before your eventual expulsion from the Assembly in 1994 at which you were no longer invited to SDS deputies' club meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What was at that point then?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Following my expulsion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, that's clear. I'm sorry if I didn't make that plain enough in my question. So up to your expulsion, there wasn't any point at which you were no longer invited; that's correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, no --

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's always an ambiguous way of putting a question, Mr. Trbojevic. What I want to ask you now is about sessions of the government, many of which you attended. And I wonder whether the witness is going to need and so will everybody else, Your Honour, the witness is going to need bundle 1 of the material produced by the Prosecution for the purposes of his evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we could give him the bundle and could you identify which tab we start at.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour. I'm going to start with tab 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Trbojevic, do you see that tab 8 is minutes of a meeting of the government of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina held on 18th May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, my first question, and refresh yourself sufficiently by the contents if you need to, is: Was that too soon for you to have attended such a meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not here. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If we turn to tab 9, and I should say, do you -- if you can't say, then tell Their Honours, but certainly from the -- the various minutes over the period, the position appears to be that for a while until sometime in June, there wasn't a record kept in the minutes of who was attending but that at some point in June, that started to be done. We're going to see that on the documents. Do you remember that, Mr. Trbojevic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. How would I remember that? I wasn't at the meeting on he 18th because I wasn't in Pale. On the 23rd, I might have been but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Let's just look at tab 9, the 23rd, to see whether the contents of those minutes enable you to have any recollection of whether you were there, taking it as quickly as you can. You see item one, the government was informed about negotiations relating to lifting of blockades of barracks in Sarajevo, decided heavy weaponry shouldn't be handed over to the enemy. Item 2 was to do with mobilisation. Item 3 to do with possibilities and opportunities for declaring state of war in the municipalities. Item 4 to do with abolition of Crisis Staffs. I won't go any further, Mr. Trbojevic, does that enable you, say if it doesn't, does it jog your mind as whether you were or were likely to have been at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
