utterances.text: Looking at the date, it might be possible but judging from the agenda, I would not really tell because the barracks were a matter of discussion for as long as they were topical, for -- until the matter was resolved, and when that was, I cannot really say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right. Well, the next tab -- we'll leave that one, then, Mr. Trbojevic. The next tab, 10, is a minute of a meeting the following day, 24th of May. But a difference here is that you are specifically mentioned. If we just go to the end of that. Do you have that tab 10, Mr. Trbojevic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You've got it? If we just go quickly to the end, the very last item, FM 5 under main item 3, the vice-president of the government Milan Trbojevic has been instructed to, in cooperation with the ministries in charge, make a list of regulations, the passing of which is priority." So would you agree, Mr. Trbojevic, it's very likely indeed that you were at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And if we look at main item 2, it's the first page in the English anyway, "It has been concluded that for the needs of the government, the Ministry of Interior should prepare a complete and scrupulous information regarding the security situation and the state of public order and peace in Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Special attention should be paid ..." et cetera, and that was done, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is -- the following conclusion is stated here, that an exhaustive report needs to be submitted on the state of public order and peace. This was a matter of discussion throughout the term of office of this government. I can't really tell you how many reports there were on this subject but that the general situation was a very poor one. I believe that this is a matter of common knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Are you saying -- I just want to put it to you fairly, Mr. Trbojevic, are you saying at the moment you can't remember whether such a complete and scrupulous report, I think is a fair translation, in fact, was produced?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe there were several such reports. If you look at the different issues that were discussed here as problems, the issue of crime, protection of public property, war profiteering, harassment of citizens and other issues relevant to the political situation and the state of the Serbian people, then it becomes quite clear to you that this is a wide range of topics that had to be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you one clarification in this respect. You're saying that it included state property, but it also says "Personal property of Serb people," and one line further, it says, "Instances of mistreatment of the citizens of Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina," and finally it says, "The evaluation of political situation and mood of Serbian people." Property of Serb people, would that include non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Based on this, one cannot conclude either way, but public security cannot be discussed while at the same time distinguishing between the property of one ethnicity and that of the other or the security of some citizens as opposed to all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you can do that, isn't it? Whether it gives a complete picture is a different matter, but you could do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I'm saying. One cannot talk about the personal security or safety of citizens by talking of one ethnicity only. One cannot talk of the safe property of members of one ethnicity without taking into account the others. That's what I was saying that there were numerous problems here that had to be dealt with and solutions had to be found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that mean that the report you were seeking, including the issue of mistreatment of the citizens of Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina would cover both mistreatment of Serbian and non-Serbian citizens?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course the report should cover both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the mood of the Serbian people, would that include the mood of the non-Serbian people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what is meant by this, believe me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Under main item three, we see as paragraph 1, "It has been agreed that Serb People Assembly Chairman Momcilo Krajisnik should set up a meeting with the leadership of Republic of Serbian Krajina in Banja Luka, Serb Autonomous Region of Krajina. The meeting should be organised as soon as possible." Are you able to tell Their Honours any more about that meeting than we see set out here in the minute?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember well, I know that there were two meetings with the leadership of the Republika Srpska Krajina, one in Banja Luka and the other, I believe, in Novi Grad. Now, who had arranged these meetings and how, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can you say what they were for? Well, let's stick with this Banja Luka meeting. Can you say what that meeting was for?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, the Republic of the Serbian Krajina was an institution of Serbs who were fighting for their rights in the Republic of Croatia. In Republika Srpska, what was strongly advocated was that we, in Republika Srpska, ought to declare a sort of a unification with the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, and this was mostly advocated by those in the Republic of the Serbian Krajina and by the Serbs in the Banja Luka area. As far as I know, Karadzic was opposed to such a view. And I believed that he even said that this was the instruction from Belgrade, that this sort of unification ought not to be advocated or declared.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So the government meeting on this occasion was aware of the issue in relation to the SAO Krajina; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is evident that a meeting was being planned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, but they were -- the government were aware of the issue, were they?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One can glean that from the minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is it your recollection or are you just gleaning it now from the minutes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember, I've just said, that the pressure of the deputies from the Bosnian Krajina was very prominent in that they were asking that Republika Srpska and the Republic of the Serbian Krajina unite. I know that the deputies of the Autonomous Region of Krajina were making some arrangements along these lines with the Republic of the Serbian Krajina and were proposing that they should declare their unification. I know also that Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not certain whether the witness said Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- was opposing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you say that you also knew that Karadzic or that Krajisnik was opposing that, the interpreters could not hear you well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that Karadzic was opposed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can you tell Their Honours the reason for the government agreeing that -- well, let me ask you this, first, when the minute says, "It has been agreed that Serb people Assembly Chairman Momcilo Krajisnik should set up a meeting," that's recording a decision of this government meeting, is it, as opposed to reporting some previous agreement with somebody outside the government?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say with any certainty; however, the government was unable to take a decision to the effect that Krajisnik was going to meet, to set up a meeting with someone. It might -- it could only have stated that Krajisnik was doing something along those lines. This is probably just a statement in the form of an information -- in the form of a piece of information informing all present that this had been arranged, agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could you just perhaps read the very first few words of that item 3, paragraph 1, just read them out loud, please, for us.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is stated, "It has been agreed that the president of the Assembly of the Serbian people, Momcilo Krajisnik, was to organise the meeting."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can you say then why, specifically, it was Mr. Krajisnik who apparently was to be invited to set up that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that this was not a government order to Krajisnik to organise the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, that's understood, you made that clear, it wasn't an order.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here that there is an agreement. It doesn't say who agreed with whom but evidently, the government had information that it had been agreed that the president of the Assembly, Krajisnik, with the leadership of the Republic of Srpska Krajina would organise this meeting. The significance of this is that the minister was asked to prepare a certain platform for those talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, it was a slightly different question. Whoever agreed, and I realise Mr. Trbojevic, we've gone as far as we can on that with your helpful answers, whoever had agreed that there should be such a meeting, my question is: Do you know why, specifically, it was Mr. Krajisnik who was to be invited or had been invited, whichever, to set up the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that question, whether Karadzic was absent or was planning to go somewhere else, or whether Krajisnik had better relations with some leaders in the Serbian Krajina, I really wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But you were indicating, and is this right, that item -- or paragraph 2, under -- it's all under this main item 3, but paragraph, 2, "It has been concluded that a dialogue platform should be prepared," that that's for the purpose of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the purpose was to be -- to inform the session of the government about that agreement. That the ministers should prepare the materials to be discussed at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, a dialogue platform -- that's not a very familiar English phrase, I've got to say. Can I try and get the sense from you, then, this is -- it was a position paper or a policy paper that was to be prepared; is that the sense of that item? Perhaps I could invite you to read it first, Mr. Trbojevic. We might get something different from interpreters from dialogue and platform, could you just read that paragraph please, paragraph 2?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "It was concluded that a platform for talks should be prepared and that the ministers should prepare contributions from their spheres of competence."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, it looks -- I keep getting this English word "platform" which, with the utmost of respect with the interpreters is not a word we use in this context -- but it looks as if what is happening is that the individual ministers are to prepare their contributions which are then to be put together in a single position paper of some sort; is that what you understand from that item?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think there was a single document. I remember that in Banja Luka, a declaration was formulated about our common aspirations, mutual support, things to that effect. That text has probably been published, but a joint document on what is termed "the platform" I don't think existed because I don't think that such a thing could be established. I said just a while ago that the deputies from the Krajina insisted that negotiations should be aimed at unifying the Republic of Srpska Krajina and the Republika Srpska, and as I said, Karadzic opposed this. As for the ministers, there were countless topics concerning practical cooperation that had to be discussed ranging from military units from one territory being on the other territory, police interventions. Then there was such things as school text books, the provision of electric power, procurement of food, and so on and so forth. And this is what the ministers were expected to make contributions on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did the government of which you were by this time a member have a view on the -- I'll call it the "Krajina question," the point on which Dr. Karadzic was opposed to this request for unification, that particular point? Did the government of which you were a member have a view?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was no standpoint that was defined --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there --

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- for the simple reason that we could not take it upon ourselves to define a standpoint before it was at least outlined by the Assembly. I remember that a declaration was drawn up with a text that contained only nice wishes, but nothing specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was anybody preventing or dissuading the government of which you were a member from reaching and expressing a view on this issue at this time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, the next tab, Mr. Trbojevic, is obviously 11, after 10. The very next tab is "minutes of government meeting of 29th of May," so it's just a few days, five days afterwards. Now, it doesn't follow as night follows day, Mr. Trbojevic, but you are mentioned, it's page 3 of the English, I'm sorry not to be able to give you the specific point in the B/C/S, but under item -- main item 3, after about ten lines or so, there's a paragraph beginning "Milan Trbojevic and Velibor Ostojic are responsible for the visits." Do you see that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't found it yet. Just a minute, please. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While the witness reads, I'd like to clarify one issue where there seems to be a problem with "platform." It seems that it's the same word as used in the B/C/S. Is that a word you would expect or is a normal expression, platform there? I'm asking this to the interpreters so ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if you would describe what a platform in these terms would be, could you -- apart from saying that's a platform, how would you describe it or am I asking too much?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: A kind of basis for discussion, perhaps, or a position paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We have to leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's extremely helpful, Your Honour. The interpreter did -- did produce there one of the phrases which I suggested, so we're ad item on that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They're experts. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- so that's extremely helpful. They are, and that's extremely helpful, Your Honour. Well, they've certainly -- well, I've got no contribution on the B/C/S, Your Honour, as Your Honour knows. The ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, you found that paragraph now, have you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, of course it's a well-known trick to give jobs to people who aren't at the meeting but I wonder whether, in this case, does that trigger off any recollection or does that lead you to be able to say that you were or very probably were at this meeting? You're referred to again, a few lines down.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say whether I was there. It's possible I was as it was nearby, but I can't remember. I do think, however, that Mr. Velibor Ostojic and I did not go to see Vogosca or Ilijas. We didn't go there, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Let's try to come at it this way, you are seen as absent from some other government meetings but when you were actually in Pale, can we take it that you would attend government meetings, in other words, absent from government meetings would signify that you were, in fact, out of Pale, is that correct? I'm putting it to you. I just want your answer on that, Mr. Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It would be unusual for me to be at Pale and not to attend a government session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's helpful, Mr. Trbojevic. And since this was the 29th of May, this was within just a couple of weeks of your arriving in Pale, are you able to remember how long it was after your arrival in Pale in May before, on any occasion, you left Pale?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you. I travelled on several occasions because of family obligations so I would leave Pale for a day or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So anyway, we don't -- well, we don't know for sure whether you're at this meeting, Mr. Trbojevic, that's the position, isn't it? Agreed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. I can't say for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you weren't at meetings, you did routinely receive the minutes of the government meetings from which you've been absent, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You indicated that you didn't go on such a visit, as is referred to here, to either the Vogosca or Ilijas, is that correct, or that you don't remember for sure?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure I didn't go to Ilijas. As for Vogosca, I went there on Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. several occasions but I think I didn't go there immediately after my arrival. I'm almost sure I didn't go there in May or in that early period. Later on, I went to Vogosca on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The time scale contemplated in this minute immediately above the first reference to your name indicates, "It's been concluded that in two days, the municipalities of Sarajevo region should be visited." Do you know whether, in fact, anybody from the government did go on those contemplated visits to, in fact, it's four municipalities, Vogosca, Ilijas, Stari Grad, and Centar?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The next paragraph after the reference to you and Mr. Ostojic and those, in fact, two other gentlemen, and then the four municipalities it says that "In the course of these visits, they should talk to the Crisis Staffs, take note of the situation, by all means visit the front, make contact with the soldiers and prepare a report about it for the government." Do you recall that being the government's approach towards this issue at meetings at this period, the end of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never went to the front line, we never visited the soldiers or talked to them, nor was it possible at all. As for the Crisis Staffs, I don't know if we even knew where all the municipalities around Sarajevo were located so that in a two-day period, that visit certainly didn't take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm going to have to seek clarification there, Mr. Trbojevic. When you said you don't know if you even knew where all the municipalities around Sarajevo were located, you mean literally, that the government didn't even know where they were or is there some misunderstanding there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm trying to say is that the government found itself on Pale in exile from the town. At that time, there were military operations going on on both sides, the demarcation line between what had been declared the Serbian municipality of Stari Grad and the Serbian municipality Centar in relation to the city centre, for example, was something that we did not know. There was a group of fighters on one side of the cemetery holding a line toward the centre of the city. On the other side of the cemetery, there was a group of fighters holding the line toward the mountain and that could be considered some kind of demarcation line, conditionally speaking. There was no way to get through from Pale to Vogosca to Ilijas. You couldn't travel that way. You had to go partly through the woods and then down streams, through the factory in Vogosca, pass through areas which were under constant sniper fire and so on and so forth. So the boundaries of the municipalities and who the representatives of each municipality were, that was very moot.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The difficulties you describe about physically getting to those municipalities, you knew of those difficulties -- I'm talking about you personally here, Mr. Trbojevic, you knew of those difficulties at this time, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A little later, not in the early period. A little later when this route was made -- when it was made possible, more or less, to travel that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, are you saying that as at the 29th of May, 1992, those difficulties of access to those municipalities existed but you didn't know about them, or that they didn't exist at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that at that time, I did not know about all of this. In the following days, I learned about all the problems I have told you about and many others which there is no point in enumerating now. You had to have a bulldozer pass through a meadow so that it could be followed by a car. You had to walk where there was a hill or a slope so as to be shielded from fire and so on and so forth, in order to arrive in Vogosca, and then from Vogosca in Ilijas.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Whatever difficulties did emerge or existed about physical access to these places, do you agree it's clear that the government view was that it was its responsibility to go to these places, to talk to the Crisis Staffs, and to take note of the situation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not in dispute. There were people living there, trying to organise life behind the front lines and of course we had to know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And there was -- in these few lines in the minute, there's a note of encouragement to visit the front and make contact with the soldiers if that should be feasible; is that a fair summary of what appears in this minute?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then the next item, paragraph 2, not the next main item, paragraph 2 there, it says, "The government has been informed about the problems with the distribution of the humanitarian aid through Dobrotvor" - it says "benefactor," then - "it has been emphasised then that this is a very serious problem and that it should be urgently solved." Do you remember what that particular problem was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember there was a humanitarian organisation called Dobrotvor, benefactor. That is to say the Vladika of the Serb Orthodox Church Nikolai would come to Pale and ask me personally to register a humanitarian organisation which is called Dobrotvor which means benefactor but you couldn't have two organisation with the same name and that is why some doubt arose as to whether those calling themselves Dobrotvor were actually abusing the name. But as far as I can remember, I don't think there were any real consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then you were designated to check how the work was legally regulated and then in the following paragraph below that big paragraph, it says, "The problem of refugees in the neighbouring republics ..." Do you see that? It's about a dozen lines on from what we've just been looking at. "The problem of refugees in the neighbouring republics has been pointed out." Do you see that paragraph, Mr. Trbojevic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: "Since the neighbouring republics has been pointed out how to keep record of them and how to make it possible for them to return to the republic as a great number of them has expressed a desire to do so." So "neighbouring republics," that's particularly referring to Croatia, is it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: "And making it possible for them to return to the republic," that republic is Republika Srpska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm moving on to the next tab, perhaps that would be ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and I would first like to ask Madam Usher to escort Mr. Trbojevic out of the courtroom. We'll have a break, Mr. Trbojevic, of 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, taking into account that we would have approximately another 55 minutes after the break, would it be possible to finish the cross-examination of the witness today or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I must say, it is -- unless something quite unexpected happens, it's extremely unlikely that I would finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I can't blame you for that, I mean you took four hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I understood, Your Honour, I wasn't being blamed, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You took four hours now, where a 60 per cent would be -- would add up the questions of the Judges being deduced, and of course it's a rough estimate, would bring you to 5 hours but 60 per cent would bring you close to 6 hours. It's a 1-hour difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I say straight away, it would be, I suggest, not a productive debate this afternoon, but Your Honour, I -- the Defence would very much reserve its position on what is the appropriate application of a 60 per cent guideline but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- until we get to that bridge, Your Honour, perhaps we shouldn't cross it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There might be an opportunity, and I would like to explore with the witness to continue Friday next week through videolink. That would save --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was very much hoping that Your Honour would not, with respect, bring up the question of videolink in relation to this witness. We have had this before, Your Honour. I'm pleased by the way that Your Honour has brought it up in the absence of the witness, may I say that straight away. Your Honour, it really is, in my submission, the Defence -- inappropriate that a witness -- this is -- in terms of his function, this witness appears to be the highest-ranking witness that the Prosecution are going to produce in the entire case unless they come up with some real surprise. He has given evidence for three and a half, three and a bit days in chief. I am in the middle of cross-examination. The witness has not indicated, apart from obviously inconvenience for Monday, he has not indicated that there is any significant problem for him in coming back to The Hague on a suitable date. Goodness knows he's been to the saying so many times because he was counsel in the Brdjanin case. It's really not an issue for him. There is simply no reason, with respect, Your Honour, for his evidence to be concluded in videolink. This is, in a sense, an occasion when some degree of confrontation between Mr. Krajisnik and -- in the civilised way in which it occurs, should take place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that the Defence opposes the idea of -- at the same time, sometimes I ask myself why we could not get the information from the witness in approximately a third of time. For example, we heard you putting a lot of questions of which, finally, I thought would come by -- would come down mainly to the question whether the government considered it its concern to go to these municipalities and speak with the people. I think -- I don't know exactly how long we spent on that and whether the roads were good or bad and finally, it results in an answer by the witness that this, of course, was something of concern for the government which is a -- of course is a good thing to know, but whether the ways that led to that answer were all necessary ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say, with respect, I have a large measure of agreement. This witness has, as many witnesses do, but this witness has given me and Your Honour an inordinate amount of information which I don't want and Your Honours probably don't want. But Your Honour, I can't -- please, Your Honour, I could, if Your Honour is inviting me to be, I could be distinctly firmer in interrupting the witness, but it's an extremely difficult thing to do, especially when interpretation is being adopted. If Your Honour wishes to do it in that situation, then I don't have any real objection. It is sometimes apparent when this witness is going into that area, but may I say this, Your Honour, this is a different point. Your Honour seems to be implying that in some way, the Defence is responsible for the witness's evidence not being finished so he has to return to Bosnia and therefore, videolink would be a fair result. Your Honour, that's not ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll not discuss this in general. The only thing I'm saying is that there are two questions. The first question is that if a government, according to its minutes, decides that people should visit certain municipalities, that one could even wonder whether it is not self-evident that the government, at that time, then thought that -- of their concern. I mean otherwise, I mean, it was not a time, it was not a situation to see whether you can spend, say, your Wednesday afternoons in a better way than going to a football match. I mean it's -- so a big question mark could already be put to the relevance of emphasising that or confirming this where it seems to be obvious from the document that they thought this of their concern. That's point one, and then the second point is whether it should really take much time to hear this from the witness. Of course the Chamber is hesitant in interfering with the answers given by the witness. But if the witness goes to details which are really not of any importance for the Defence, then of course he should be stopped and he should be put direct questions on what the Defence would like to know. So the Chamber in considering all matters at this time, that is the way in which a witness is examined, also includes in its assessment not having led to any conclusions at this moment, also includes in its assessment the efficiency and how the witness is examined. We'll adjourn until ten minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we restart, Mr. Stewart, triggered by your observation on the 60 per cent rule, the Chamber has used the last break to also discuss the efficiency of cross-examination. It has -- it takes the position that any relevant information elicited from the witness during the last hour and a half could have been elicited from him in approximately a third, and if we would be very generous, half of the time, therefore, the Chamber will further pay specific attention to the efficiency of the cross-examination and we'll do that to start with right now also in order to see whether it is true that the 60 per cent rule should be reconsidered. We'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, Your Honour always referred to it as a "rule," we had always understood it's a guideline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To see whether it's true that the 60 per cent guideline would need to be reconsidered. Madam Usher, would you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, may I give you an advance apology. I may, from time to time, interrupt you in your answer, if it appears that perhaps we're getting into an area where the information is not directly useful to the Trial Chamber or is not, in fact, what I am seeking by my questions. So I hope you will forgive me if sometimes I might appear to be slightly abrupt. I'm not meaning to be rude, I'm trying to achieve more efficiency. Could you take tab 12, please, Mr. Trbojevic. This is a minute of government meeting of the 30th of May, 1992. Item 1 over the page on the English, so it's probably on the second page in the B/C/S, but it's main item 1, "it's been concluded it's necessary the government be informed about everything that takes place in the republic and outside it about the negotiations that are with regard to the status of internal system about ministry strategy," and so on. And then a number of issues are mentioned, important some of them. Finishing up, "Government should creatively participate in determining the attitudes about those issues and it should work on realisation that the agreed-upon policy within its constitution and legal rights and authority." And then there's a reference to "... overlapping of jurisdictions which has a negative impact on the work of the government ministries and other republic and state institutions." Is this a reflection of the sort of anarchy, to use that broad word that you used and disorganisation that we were considering earlier?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this is more or less consistent with what I have been saying so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- then there's a reference to "Bearing this in mind, it has been suggested that the meeting of the Presidency Assembly and government should be sped up." Do you have any recollection of such a meeting at this specific time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Assembly sessions were most often attended by the government and the Presidency in those cases when all of them were available. Almost every Assembly session was of that kind, meaning that they -- that it was attended by both government members and Presidency members as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then it's item 16, current issues, and then about five or six paragraphs down in that there is a reference to, "The ministries which haven't already done that should submit the proposals, the platform for dialogue with Serbian Republic of Krajina and SAO Bosanska Krajina." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, do you remember whether your ministry had already submitted a proposal at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have a ministry of my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. That's all right, I'll withdraw that. Over the page, the very last item in the minute refers to "An agreement about giving guarantees for safety of flight control workers at Sarajevo airport should be reached at the joint meeting of the Presidency, Assembly president and government." Was the reason for that being suggested to be dealt with at that joint meeting because it was an important issue and there was that meeting coming up. Was that the reason?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about these flight control workers at the Sarajevo airport. I know nothing of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on then to tab 13. Under item 1, there's a list of the items in the usual way that was adopted and then item 1, it's the second page of the English version, "The proposal of the law on amendments on constitutional law" is the first paragraph. Then on the next one, "The proposal of the decisions to form War Presidencies in municipalities during the immediate threat of war or the state of war has been approved provided that ..." and so on. That was a government decision then, was it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have reason to doubt it; it is stated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then item 2, "The proposal of the law on national defence has been determined. It has been concluded that it should be given to the president of the Presidency for signing as soon as possible." Was that something you were actively involved in, the drafting and presentation of this proposal?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's something missing in this text here. It says that the bill was drafted and that it should be forwarded for signature to the president of the Republic and then to be prepared for the publication in the Official Gazette. It seems as if the law was not at all to be passed FOR the adoption to the Assembly. Perhaps, in fact, this was the case. I only know that I was consulted at the time of the drafting of the bill.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I offer one clarification? You say the president of the republic, it reads the president of the Presidency and am I correct in understanding.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's also what the B/C/S version says.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Item 15, if you can go on that far, please. "The ministry of interior has informed the government about the current issues in the political and security situation in the republic about the degree of public order and peace and about other issues of importance for the safety in the republic. Regarding this issue, it has been concluded that the government is not sufficiently informed about the issues relevant to its work, especially about the situation in the front. It has been concluded that the government must be regularly informed about the said issues through the Ministry of Defence, Main Staff, and the Ministry of the Interior in order to be able to within its rights and authorities engage in formulating policy." Was this presented to the relevant ministers, Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Subotic, as a criticism of them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is stated here that the Minister of the Interior had submitted a report and that, in principle, the government had not been kept informed to a satisfactory degree so that this is some sort of criticism, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you remember it as being a criticism of your ministerial colleagues that they were being told by you, "You, ministers, you must ensure that we are better informed." Is that the way it was discussed and presented?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot quote the different discussions and what somebody said at which government session. I can hardly remember every single discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, if the answer is you don't remember, then the answer is, please, you don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you move to the next document, I don't know whether you do, Mr. Stewart, I would have one very short question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You told us that the proposal of the law on amendments -- no, the proposal of the decisions to form War Presidencies in the municipality was a government proposal. Do you remember whether it was also the government's initiative to propose this or was it the initiative of any other body that could take such initiatives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that there exists a government decision or an instruction dating from April. That was prior to my arrival there, and I don't know how this decision came about. Here, what is discussed are the amendments to the law, the constitution is invoked, and War Presidencies are mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "The proposal of the decisions to form War Presidencies in municipalities during the immediate threat of war or the state of war has been approved." Whose initiative was it that led to the proposal of the decisions to form War Presidencies? Do you know it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I assure you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can we go to tab 14, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We see under item number 1, I think it is, it's -- well, yes, it Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. is, it's on the second page of the English, so it's probably somewhere on the second page of the B/C/S. Do you see -- this is not the point, but just to get the reference, do you see something referring to the law on stamps? Law on salaries, law on stamps, do you see that place?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then a couple of lines after that, we get, "The government once again concluded that it's not informed about the current political and military issues and about the situation in the republic. It has been concluded that the government should be informed about those issues on daily basis and that that should be the first item on the agenda. In order to make that possible, a constant contact with the Main Staff should be maintained through the government president and the Ministry of Defence. A good system of communication between the government bodies and army command should also be provided." Now, did Mr. Djeric, in accordance with what was being said clearly there by the government, did Mr. Djeric then, himself, make an attempt to maintain that constant contact with the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you know that he didn't or is it just that you're not aware that he did?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware that he did, but I believe that one can infer from these numerous minutes that he was not in a position to convey the information to the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And as far as the Ministry of Defence is concerned then, it was being clearly said here by you and your government colleagues that, "Constant contact should be maintained through the Ministry of Defence as well." Do you remember, was the position that, in the view of the government, there was insufficient contact between the Ministry of Defence and the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that an assessment to that effect was made because as far as I know. The Defence Minister did not give any specific account of this relationship to the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was the question then of where the -- the flaw in the communication of information lay investigated any more than these minutes imply?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then the very last item in this minute, "It has been concluded that a non-stop on-duty duty should be introduced into the government president's cabinet and that the persons on duty would be determined by the ministries according to the established roster." Did -- it was the ministers who were to rotate in this duty; is that what it's saying?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that a duty officer had to be there at the secretariat of the government and the ministries were supposed to provide the staff to rotate in these duty stints.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So it wasn't the ministers themselves who were necessarily to rotate on duty, but somebody was to be on duty; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, including the ministers but also others from the ministries.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of this round the clock, I suppose, what was the purpose of this round-the-clock duty?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simply to have a person, an alert person in the building all the time so that in the event of a piece of information reaching the building, there would be someone to receive it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did it specifically have in mind military matters?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any and all matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, were military matters at the top of the list of concerns which led to this decision?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think the military matters were included there at all because the military does not talk in any open way with a civilian administrative officer responding on the other end of the line. I think that the Defence Minister had his own contacts with the Main Staff, and I'm not referring now to the government telephone lines. I believe that he had lines other than those.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Let's turn to the next tab, please, which is number 15. Item 8, "It has been agreed that a platform for the dialogue in Herzegovina should be prepared. Proposals for the platform should be submitted by all of the ministries. The proposals should emphasise what has been done on the republic level, what they have done so far. Concrete problems and suggestions about what should be done so that the government and economy in SAO Herzegovina would function. The delegation members and the deadline will be determined later on." Mr. Trbojevic, was there, in practice, difficulty about getting such work out of the ministries?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not difficult for the ministries to plan their activities. What is mentioned here in this text is the need to establish connections with the SAO Herzegovina because this autonomous district of Herzegovina practically ceased to exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then item 12, there is a reference to the reports from the official visits to -- well, that Foca, SAO Semberija, Majevica, and Krajina have been accepted. Do you remember those were official visits by whom, can you say?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then the next tab, 16, 5th of June, 1992, we do see that change of format where, from now on, -- I couldn't swear without exception, but we can see, from now on there is a record of those attending, you will see that, the 5th of June, 1992. And you're included there. Item 1, "Government president has informed the government about the current issues of security situation in the republic, the information is based on the daily reports from the Ministry of Interior." Were such daily reports in writing?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One type of these daily reports was the one that I had occasion to see, and these were police reports enumerating different events. You know the way the police usually put it: At such and such an hour, there was this and this event. It called for intervention or it did not call for an intervention. They call them dispatches. So it is possible that this here is the case of one such report. I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But Mr. Trbojevic, are you saying this item 1 refers to that sort of very specific local report, if you like, rather than a more general report on the security situation in the republic as a whole?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It is possible that the information contained therein originated from all the different areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The item 11, second paragraph under item 11, "Once again, the government pointed out the need to consider and undertake the measures to secure wider area of Pale and especially the objects which housed the state bodies. It has been concluded that the Ministry of Interior and the security bodies of the Main Staff of the Serbian People's Army should analyse the mentioned problem and undertake necessary measures." So the -- the government concludes that somebody should be done by the Main Staff. Was that then transmitted direct from the government to the Main Staff or by the Minister of Defence to the Main Staff as a government order?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Minister of Defence had to pass it on to the Main Staff because it concerned the security of the place in which the government and the other organs or bodies were meeting. It had to be secured so that there would be no breakthrough by enemy units from the direction of Mount Jahorina and from Kalinovic, the -- in that direction, there were no facilities or units of the Serb army and so on. After this, I know that a platoon was established to provide security for the government and the government employees, a reserve unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We'll move on to item 13, please. "The government has been informed," and I'm looking not at milking cows or coins, I'm looking at Security Council meeting that's the third one down, about the possibility that there might be another Security Council meeting, the purpose of which would be shedding the light on the manipulations with the report of Boutros-Gali, UN Secretary General, and consequently that there might be a congress meeting in the U.S." Was the government informed about this matter by Mr. Djeric or did it receive information from somebody else outside the government?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember who specifically said this. It might have come from the Presidency or Djeric brought it from the Presidency after talking to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But you don't know where it came from?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Tab 17, please, the 7th of June government meeting. You are present again. And then item 6 is the report of the Sarajevo Crisis Staff, though it actually becomes item 7 when we -- it's just a misnumbering, there isn't an item 6. So 5 to 7. 7, "The government has acknowledged the report of the Sarajevo Crisis Staff." That was a written report, was it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And do you recall, was it a report to the government?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably it was because it was discussed at the government session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, just commenting tab 18, we can go over, it's 8th of June and you were not present and I don't want to ask you anything about that. Tab 19, minutes of a meeting on the 9th of June. Item 1 subitem B, "The government acknowledged the letter" item A is the government supported an order for the central committee of the exchange of the prisoners." B, "the government acknowledged the letter of correspondence from the president of central committee for the exchange of prisoners. It has been concluded that the minister of [illegible] should talk to Rajko Colovic," can you see what ministry it is on the B/C/S version? We've got "illegible" in the English, but presumably it's illegible in your language as well, is it? Can you see?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it says minister of justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: "It has been concluded that the Minister of Justice" as you suggested it is, "Should take to Rajko Colovic, the ministry president, to as to determine what sort of motives for suggesting the change," and so on. Are you aware of any contact between Mr. Colovic and Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So would it surprise you in any way if you were told that there never was any contact between Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Colovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then item 20 or tab 20, we can go over, it was a meeting at which you were present.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, I'm not suggesting there's nothing relevant but nothing that requires cross-examination, of course, which is an entirely different question. The -- well, often a different question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The same applies to tab 21, Mr. Trbojevic. You were, in fact, absent from that meeting but there's nothing I wish to ask you arising out of that meeting. Tab 22 is a meeting on the 13th of June. The current issues -- well, no, but item 6, first. Item 6, "The government has ratified the treaty number 3 of the International Red Cross Committee." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, without going into painful detail, is that constitutes a legal position that it was for the government to ratify such treaties, that's correctly reflected by this minute, is it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government could institutionally not ratify. It was not competent to do that. It could only approve if one of the ministers signed this, whether it was Mr. Kalinic, I don't know. The government could agree or approve but no official formal ratification was provided for.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, what -- if anybody, what was the appropriate organ, then, or the appropriate constitutional process for ratification of a treaty?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It was usual for international treaties to be ratified by the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You chaired this meeting, didn't you, Mr. Trbojevic, as it's shown?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that I chaired the meeting but I'm telling you in connection with what it says here, it probably means that the government agreed with the text someone had brought in and accepted the signature, and this has to do with providing security for a humanitarian convoy which is not in dispute. But to use the word "ratify" is a bit too much in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right. Item 7, current issues, "It has been concluded that the Minister of Foreign Affairs should send a already of protest to the permanent members of the Security Council." Was that a conclusion, a decision made by the government without having to seek anybody else's approval?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the Minister of Foreign Affairs to issue a protest, no approval was required here by anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then at the foot of that page in the English, the paragraph begins, it's the third paragraph down under item 7, "The question of having a joint meeting of the government and the republic Presidency has been brought up once more. Reason for this has been the conclusion that the government is not sufficiently informed about the most important issues and that therefore it cannot participate in determining the policy and making of the vital decisions which is its legal right and duty." Can you recall what, in your view, was the most important issue on the top of the list of issues at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't separate out only one or two issues. I can't really make a list of all the issues, but this was something that was a problem throughout this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on, then, to tab 23, another meeting chaired by you. Did something similar apply in the case of Mr. Djeric that if Mr. Djeric was not at a meeting, would that, in practice, indicate that he was not in Pale?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then tab 24, again -- Mr. Djeric is present chairing that matter. We can go on to 25 which is 29th session of the government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps Judge Hanoteau would like to put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry for interrupting. I'd like us to come back to tab 22, page 3. The last sentence read out to you by Mr. Stewart [In English]" ... of the government and republic Presidency has been brought up once more. The reason for this has been the conclusion that the government is not sufficiently informed." [Interpretation] What does it mean? Maybe my English is not quite good enough, but when I read this text, my first impression is that it is suggested that it is necessary to hold a meeting, the government wants a meeting with the Presidency. The government complains because it is not sufficiently informed. Does that mean that the Presidency itself was better informed than the government? Was that the issue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, the government wanted to go to the Presidency to say, "We are not sufficiently informed."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then why was the Presidency better informed than the government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The members of the Presidency, I've already spoken about this, went to Belgrade. They met with international representatives. They went out on the ground. We spent a lot more time at the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How was it that the Presidency was everywhere on the ground? How was it, because they had people on the ground, that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Presidency had its own people and these are not people that the government could say they could not cooperate with, but it's a fact that through the party and through the offices they held, they were able to get much more information than we in the government felt we were getting. And on several occasions, a meeting of the Presidency and the government was arranged and it was postponed every time because the members of the Presidency were out in the field, a meeting could not be held, and this went on and on and on. It went on until that final Assembly session in May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What do you mean by the people from the Presidency, who were they, according to you? You say they were in the field.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am speaking of Dr. Karadzic, Mrs. Plavsic, Mr. Koljevic, and Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That means that they went in the field more than the others. They went in the field personally; is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. Mr. Krajisnik less than the others, but the other three, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's one small thing that's not clear to me yet. One of your answers was that the Presidency had its own people and these are not people that the government could not say they could not cooperate with but it's a fact that through the party, and through the offices they held, they were able to get much more information than we in the government felt we were getting." Are you talking about its own people, these people? Do I understand your answer correctly that these were people in the party spread all over the territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am referring primarily to the infrastructure of the party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And would that include Crisis Staffs, War Presidencies, or would you exclude that from the party infrastructure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I wouldn't exclude that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stewart, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Me too, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The miracle did not happen, I take it, or if you would say, well, I've got still -- of course you had a far higher speed, if you would say still a couple to go, that would be finished in 10 to 15 minutes then I could address the interpreters. If not, I'd like to hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, the circumstances for your addressing the interpreters will not arise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Trbojevic, unfortunately we are not able to finish your examination by today. You informed us that you have to be on Monday in court which is, of course, a perfect excuse for not being here. Could you tell us about the second half of next week, whether you would be available, especially Thursday/Friday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On Monday, I am sure I have to be in Sarajevo. As for my other obligations in the course of the week, those can be postponed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We are specifically thinking about next Friday and there are a few options. One of them being that you would return to The Hague and that your cross-examination would be -- that you would further be cross-examined. Another way of doing that would be through videolink. Is any of them more suitable to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, to tell you the truth, I don't know what it looks like by videolink. I do not want to cause any problems. Whatever is simpler to organise, it's up to you to decide. I assume it would be easier by videolink from Banja Luka or Sarajevo but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, videolink is for some people easier for others, it's not, both in terms of organisation and ... We'd like to consider that and we'll let you know not later than by Monday whether that would be suitable to you what we'd like, but if you could try to keep your agenda so flexible for the second half of next week.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then you are excused for this moment. Since you are still to finish your examination -- your testimony, you are again instructed not to speak with anyone about your testimony you have given and you are still about to give soon. Madam Usher, would you escort Mr. Trbojevic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, could you give us any indication on how much time you'd still need at the pace you developed over the last hour?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, obviously as one goes through a series of similar documents, inevitably the same ground crops up, so one speaks up. So far as the government minutes are concerned, that won't take very much longer. Your Honour, I -- there's a pretty good chance that I'm going to come in within the 60 per cent guidelines, I would say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would mean approximately not more than one additional hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Probably Your Honours and I would calculate the 60 per cent guideline differently but not more than a couple of hours, I would think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we do some bookkeeping.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour that is quite a -- potentially if it should arise in the future, the question of what the 60 per cent guideline means where there has been several days of examination with counsel's questions and the Bench's questions all mixed in together is -- does require some very careful consideration rather than some simple mathematical calculation of the type that's being hinted at by the Trial Chamber over the last few days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mathematics is not a purpose in itself, it is to assist us and gives only one aspect of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I heartily endorse that view, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't hear it and I can't read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No -- we -- I said we heartily endorse that view, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And heartily and hardly is --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Heartily, with all my heart, Your Honour, I endorse that view, since it's Friday, Your Honour, it's -- I would go that far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, it is a very comforting last words before we adjourn until next Monday, 9.00 in the morning in this same courtroom. We'll then also decide on how to proceed with Mr. Trbojevic. If there's nothing else urgent on the agenda, I would like to thank the interpreters and technicians for again another 7 stolen minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 11th day of April, 2005, at 9.00 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.08 p.m.,
